response.original_text: His work helped defend the Philippines. American marine biologist Dr. Kent Carpenter, whose scientific testimony supported the Philippines in its landmark 2016 South China Sea arbitration case against China, was shot and killed during a home invasion in Negros Oriental province in the Central Visayas region of the Philippines. Police said three unidentified men forcibly entered Carpenter's home in Barangay Ajong, Sibulan, on the night of July 12. One of the intruders allegedly shot the 73-year-old scientist in the head, killing him. His 34-year-old companion was also injured. The suspects remain at large, and investigators are reviewing CCTV footage, interviewing witnesses, and pursuing leads. Police Brigadier General Romano Cardiño condemned the killing as a "senseless act of violence" and vowed to bring those responsible to justice. Carpenter was widely respected in the scientific community for his decades of work in the Philippines. He first began studying the country's marine ecosystems in 1975 and became one of the world's leading experts on Philippine marine biodiversity. Beyond his scientific achievements, Carpenter also played a significant role in one of the Philippines' biggest international legal victories. During the South China Sea arbitration initiated by the Philippines in 2013, he submitted expert written evidence documenting the environmental damage caused by China's island reclamation and destructive fishing practices in the West Philippine Sea. He also delivered oral testimony during the 2015 merits hearing. The tribunal's 2016 ruling overwhelmingly favored the Philippines and found no legal basis for China's sweeping "nine-dash line" claims. Carpenter also conducted extensive research in the Verde Island Passage, often called the "center of the center" of global marine shore fish biodiversity, and was a strong advocate for having the area recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. His death has prompted tributes from Silliman University, the University of the Philippines Marine Science Institute, conservation groups, and fellow scientists. Many remembered him not only as a world-class researcher, but also as a generous mentor who spent five decades helping Filipinos better understand and protect their country's extraordinary marine ecosystems. His life reminds us that science can shape history just as much as politics or diplomacy—and that the people behind those contributions are often remembered long after the headlines fade.

MANILA — Tributes and calls for justice continue to pour in following the killing of renowned marine biologist Dr. Kent Carpenter, who was found dead inside his home in Sibulan, Negros Oriental on Sunday.

Scientists, environmental groups, and conservation advocates are mourning the loss of a researcher whose decades of work helped transform the understanding and protection of the Philippines' rich marine biodiversity. Greenpeace Philippines described Carpenter's death as a significant loss at a time when the country's seas are increasingly threatened by climate change, plastic pollution, and biodiversity loss. "At a time when the worsening plastic and climate crises continue to threaten our seas and the communities that depend on them, we need more people like Dr. Kent who champion the protection of our environment and stand with communities," the group said. Carpenter's connection to the Philippines began in the 1970s after earning his biology degree. Assigned by the Peace Corps to work as a researcher with the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), he later described the assignment as the best job he had during his Peace Corps service. Partner of slain US marine biologist now among 'persons of interest' His work in the country led him to collaborate with National Scientist Dr. Angel Alcala, one of the pioneers of marine conservation in the Philippines. Their partnership helped shape decades of research on coral reefs, reef fishes, and marine ecosystems. Carpenter also developed close ties with Silliman University, where he mentored Filipino scientists and opened opportunities for local researchers to collaborate with international institutions. Dr. Robert Guino-o of Silliman University, who considered Carpenter his mentor, remembered him not only for his scientific expertise but also for his compassion toward students and coastal communities. ”I remember he would sit down and take the time to listen to concerns ranging from research or personal concerns before he would give his advice," Guino-o said. "He will be sorely missed talaga sa Silliman and certainly a big loss to the scientific community. He has this care for students, fisherfolks, fish vendors. He's good at Tagalog and a bit of Cebuano. These are traits that really endeared him to many people.” The University of the Philippines Marine Science Institute also paid tribute to Carpenter, highlighting his pioneering studies on Philippine coral reefs, reef fishes, and fisheries that laid the foundation for modern coral reef ecology in the country. According to the institute, Carpenter's research helped establish the Philippines as the "center of the center of marine shore fish biodiversity," a global recognition of the country's unparalleled diversity of reef fishes. He also strongly advocated for the protection of the Verde Island Passage, one of the world's most biologically diverse marine ecosystems, pushing for its designation as a National Protected Area and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Beyond marine biodiversity research, Carpenter also played a key role in the Philippines' arbitration case against China over the West Philippine Sea.
Environmental groups said Carpenter's legacy extended far beyond scientific publications.

Silliman University (SU), where Carpenter was a research associate, said "We join his family, colleagues, students, and the international scientific community in mourning the loss of an exceptional scientist whose life’s work advanced the understanding and conservation of marine biodiversity around the world."
The Marine Science Institute of the University of the Philippines Diliman (UP MSI) expressed gratitude for Carpenter’s “fifty years of guidance and companionship.”

“Since UP MSI’s early beginnings as a research center, Dr. Carpenter has been a great friend to the Institute, and he continues to be an enduring influence on many other marine scientists, fisherfolk organizations, and conservation groups,” UP MSI said in a statement on Tuesday.

His 34-year-old companion was also injured.
The suspects remain at large, and investigators are reviewing CCTV footage, interviewing witnesses, and pursuing leads.
